_meta.purpose: Two things: (1) the onboarding question flow that collects just enough to compute both regimes; (2) the row spec for the two-column old-vs-new comparison screen.
_meta.design_principle: Ask the minimum needed to make the comparison correct. Every question below either changes the arithmetic or changes which deductions are offered. Nothing is asked for curiosity.

onboarding_flow._note: Progressive disclosure. Stage 1 alone produces a usable answer for ~70% of salaried users. Stages 2 and 3 unlock only if the user's answers make them relevant.

stage_1_essentials.q: Which financial year are you computing for?
stage_1_essentials.why: Rates are identical, but the governing Act, section numbers and terminology differ. The chatbot and citations depend on this.

stage_1_essentials.q: Are you a resident of India for tax purposes?
stage_1_essentials.why: The s.87A/s.156 rebate is available ONLY to resident individuals. NRIs also lose the grandfathered 20%-with-indexation property option.
Old regime basic exemption is Rs 2.5L / Rs 3L / Rs 5L by age. The new regime is Rs 4L for everyone. Also drives 80D, 80DDB, 80TTA vs 80TTB and the advance-tax exemption.

stage_1_essentials.q: Where does your income come from?
stage_1_essentials.why: Business/professional income LOCKS your regime choice (one round trip for life). It also triggers the s.44AB audit and presumptive-tax paths.

stage_1_essentials.q: What is your gross annual salary (before any deductions)?
What is your annual Basic + Dearness Allowance?
stage_1_essentials.hint: Usually 40-50% of gross salary. Check your payslip.
stage_1_essentials.why: DRIVES TWO OF THE BIGGEST NUMBERS: the HRA exemption formula and the 80CCD(2) employer-NPS cap (10% vs 14%). Do not estimate this; ask for it.

stage_1_essentials.q: Any other income? (interest, dividends, rent, freelance)

stage_2_old_regime_inputs._note: Only worth asking if the old regime is plausibly competitive. Rule of thumb: if total deductions would need to exceed roughly Rs 8L for the old regime to win at higher incomes, most users can skip this. But ASK ANYWAY for anyone with a home loan or HRA - those two alone can flip the answer.

questions.q: Do you receive House Rent Allowance?
How much annual rent do you pay?
questions.show_if: hra_received > 0 OR user does not own a home

questions.q: Which city do you live in?
questions.why: Metro cities get 50% of salary in the HRA formula, non-metro 40%. FROM FY 2026-27 the metro list is reported to expand from 4 to 8 cities (adding Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad) - see the warning in deductions.json.

questions.q: How much did you invest in 80C instruments? (PPF, ELSS, EPF, life insurance, home loan principal, children's tuition)
Did you contribute to NPS yourself?
questions.sub: 80CCD(1B) gives an extra Rs 50,000 above the Rs 1.5L cap

questions.q: Health insurance premium for yourself and family?
Health insurance premium for your parents?
Home loan interest paid this year?
Is that property self-occupied or let out?
questions.why: CRITICAL. Self-occupied interest is capped at Rs 2L and is old-regime only. Let-out interest is uncapped and survives in the new regime - but the resulting loss is stranded in the new regime.

questions.q: Annual rent received?
Education loan interest paid?
Donations made to registered charities?
Interest earned on savings accounts and deposits?
Do you or a dependant have a certified disability?

stage_3_both_regimes._note: These matter in BOTH regimes. Skipping them is the single most common source of a wrong comparison.

questions.q: Does your employer contribute to your NPS account? How much annually?
questions.flag: HIGH IMPACT. Deductible in BOTH regimes. In the new regime the cap is 14% of Basic+DA for everyone; in the old regime it is 10% for private employers. This alone can swing the comparison by tens of thousands.

questions.q: Is your employer government or private?
Total annual employer contribution to PF + superannuation + NPS combined?
questions.flag: Anything above Rs 7,50,000 becomes a taxable perquisite in BOTH regimes, plus the accretion on the excess.

questions.q: Do you have a company car or employer-provided driver?
questions.flag: TAXPAYER-NEGATIVE from FY 2026-27. Perquisite values rose sharply (Rs 1,800 to Rs 5,000/month for a small car). Applies in both regimes.

questions.q: Does your employer provide accommodation?
Did you sell any shares, mutual funds or property this year?
questions.flag: Capital gains are taxed at SPECIAL rates in both regimes and are NOT covered by the s.87A rebate. A user at Rs 11L salary plus Rs 1L STCG still pays tax on the STCG.

questions.q: Do you have losses carried forward from earlier years?
questions.flag: If yes, especially house property or business losses, the old regime can be worth far more than a slab comparison shows. Surface an explicit warning.

questions.q: Which regime did you use last year?
questions.why: If the user has business income and has already switched once, the old regime may be permanently unavailable to them.

comparison_screen_rows._note: Each row renders as: Parameter | Old Regime | New Regime. Group by section. Show a running subtotal after each group.

rows.param: Add: Perquisites (car, accommodation, excess employer contribution)
House property loss set-off against salary

rows.old: One opt-out and one return, then locked for life

break_even_guidance._note: Useful as a headline answer before the detailed comparison loads. These are indicative, not exact - the true break-even depends on the exact deduction mix.
break_even_guidance.rule_of_thumb: The new regime wins unless the user's total old-regime deductions and exemptions exceed roughly the difference created by the wider new-regime slabs. Compute both; never guess.
the_four_things_that_flip_it_to_old: HRA on a large rent in a metro city
Home loan interest on a self-occupied property (up to Rs 2L)
Carried-forward house property or business losses
break_even_guidance.the_one_thing_that_flips_it_to_new: Large employer NPS contribution for a private-sector employee - 14% in the new regime versus 10% in the old
